Current, Resistance and Ohm's Law: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = delta Q / delta t, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s). Conventional current flows from positive to negative. Ohm's law says that for an ohmic conductor V = I R, where R is the resistance in ohms. The resistance of a wire is R = rho L / A, where rho is the resistivity of the material, L the length and A the cross-sectional area; metals have a resistance that rises with temperature. The drift velocity of electrons is very small, but the electric field spreads at nearly the speed of light, so a lamp lights at once. A graph of V against I for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin.
Series and Parallel Circuits: In a series circuit the components are connected one after another: the same current flows through all, the voltages add (V = V1 + V2 + ...) and the resistances add: R = R1 + R2 + ... In a parallel circuit the components are connected across the same two points: the voltage is the same across each, the currents add (I = I1 + I2 + ...) and 1 / R = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + ... The total resistance of a parallel combination is smaller than the smallest resistor. Household circuits are in parallel so that each device gets the full voltage and works independently. Ammeters are connected in series and voltmeters in parallel.
Electric Power, Energy and EMF: Electric power is the rate of energy transfer: P = I V = I^2 R = V^2 / R, in watts. The energy used is E = P t; the kilowatt-hour is 3.6 x 10^6 J. A battery has an electromotive force (emf), the energy given per coulomb, and an internal resistance r, so the terminal voltage is V = emf - I r. The current in a simple circuit is I = emf / (R + r). Maximum power is delivered to a load when R = r. Fuses and circuit breakers protect circuits from too much current. Power lost in transmission lines is I^2 R, so high voltage is used to lower the current.
Kirchhoff's Rules and Complex Circuits: Kirchhoff's rules analyze circuits that cannot be simplified. The junction rule (conservation of charge) says the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving. The loop rule (conservation of energy) says that the sum of the potential changes around any closed loop is zero: going through a battery from - to + adds emf, and going through a resistor in the direction of the current gives a drop of I R. Write one equation per independent loop and junction, then solve the equations for the unknown currents. A negative answer means that the actual current is opposite to the assumed direction. These rules also explain voltage dividers, where V_out = V_in R2 / (R1 + R2).
RC Circuits and Capacitors in Circuits: When a capacitor charges through a resistor the charge builds up gradually: Q = Q_max (1 - e^(-t / RC)), and when it discharges Q = Q0 e^(-t / RC). The time constant tau = R C (in seconds) is the time for the capacitor to charge to about 63% of its maximum or to discharge to about 37%. After 5 time constants the capacitor is essentially fully charged or discharged. Initially a discharged capacitor acts as a short circuit and, after a long time, as an open circuit (no current). Capacitors in a circuit store energy 1/2 C V^2. RC circuits are used in timers, flashing lights and filters.
